subject: MGMT160
title: Controlling: Performance, Information and Control Systems

questions.stem: Describe controlling.
options: Monitoring performance to ensure goals are achieved — 'are we meeting our goals?'
Watching employees closely during the shift to catch mistakes before customers notice them
Setting the goals and standards for next year, with a number and a date for each one
Telling staff what to do and checking that every instruction has been carried out
questions.why: Planning sets the goals; controlling checks the progress. Goals nobody checks are wishes. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Explain the first question a manager should ask when a gap appears.
options: 'Why?' — not 'who?'
'Who is to blame?'
'Who can we fire?'
'Can we hide this number?'
questions.why: A culture where measurement means punishment produces hidden numbers, not better ones. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter calls problems 'leaks'.
options: They are cheap when found early and catastrophic when found late
They always come from the plumbing of the organisation — its systems and procedures
They cannot be fixed once they have started, so the manager's job is to prevent them
They only happen in restaurants and hotels, where the customer sees the work directly
questions.why: Control systems are how managers find problems early. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Identify the four steps of the control process in order.
options: Set standards → measure performance → compare results → take corrective action
Measure performance → identify the person responsible → report upward → set a new standard
Take corrective action → set standards → measure performance → compare results
Compare results → set standards → take corrective action → measure performance
questions.why: Step 4 feeds back into step 1; the loop never ends. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Explain when controlling actually begins.
options: During planning, when the standard is set
After the first customer complaint shows that something has gone wrong
At the end of the year, when the results are compared with the budget
When the manager first notices that the team is not working as hard as it should
questions.why: Step 1's secret: controlling begins during planning, when 'good' is defined in numbers. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Describe a KPI.
options: One of the vital few measures that matter most for the goal
Every number the company can collect from its systems, so that nothing is missed
The salary and bonus of the key employees who drive the company's results
A report written once a year that summarises the company's performance for investors
questions.why: KPIs are the vital few that tell you the truth fast. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Identify the three parts of the KPI test.
options: Connected to the goal; measurable regularly from a real source; something the team can influence
Easy to count; impressive when shown to the boss; kept confidential from the team
Large enough to matter; new to the organisation; expensive enough to be taken seriously
Reported daily to the frontline; weekly to middle managers; monthly to the top
questions.why: All three must hold or the KPI is decoration. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Describe a leading indicator.
options: A measure that warns early, before the headline number drops
The most important number in the annual report, which the leadership team reports first
A KPI set personally by the leader rather than by the finance department
A measure of the leader's own performance, used to decide the leader's bonus
questions.why: Gym members who stop coming quietly stop paying three months later — visits per week warns first. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Identify three ways too much measurement harms, according to the chapter.
options: People optimise the number not the goal; the unmeasured disappears; constant monitoring signals distrust
Costs rise because of the software; computers crash under the data; reports get too long to read
Managers get bored with the dashboards; staff learn to game the bonus; customers leave for competitors
Nothing — more measurement is always better, because a manager cannot control what is not counted
questions.why: Measure calls per hour and calls get shorter — and ruder. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Explain the question data cannot answer.
options: WHY people did it, or whether it was right — data says WHAT with precision
What happened today
How many customers came, because many customers pay in cash and are not recorded
Which product sold most, because sales are recorded by department and not by item
questions.why: The metric can improve while the mission dies. Measure the vital few — and go and look. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Identify the three qualities of good feedback.
options: Timely, constructive, specific
Loud, public, frequent
Written, formal, annual
Short, polite, general
questions.why: Feedback about March delivered in December is archaeology; feedback aims at the work and names the exact behaviour and standard. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Identify the three types of control by timing.
options: Feedforward (before), concurrent (during), feedback (after)
Strict, medium and loose
Daily, weekly and monthly
Top, middle and frontline
questions.why: The earlier the control, the cheaper the fix; the later, the more it teaches next time. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Describe feedforward control.
options: Preventing problems before work starts — checking ingredients before cooking, training staff before opening
Correcting problems while the work happens — a supervisor coaching the team during the lunch rush
Learning from completed results — reviewing the month's complaints to improve next month
Checking the budget at year end to see whether the department spent more than it was given
questions.why: Cheapest fix: the problem never happens. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Describe the chapter's calibrated answer to 'can managers control too much?'.
options: Not less control — better-placed control: tight on outcomes and safety, loose on method
Yes — remove all controls, because trained people perform best when they are trusted completely
No — control everything, always, because a manager is accountable for every result
Control only new employees closely; experienced staff should never be measured
questions.why: Measure the result the customer feels; let the trained person choose the how. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Identify the five parts of a control plan.
options: Three vital-few KPIs with standards; a source and frequency for each; one immediate fix; one system fix; a feedback rule and a monitoring line you will not cross
A budget for the year; a chart of who does what; a slogan for the team; a reward for the best performer; a report to head office at the end of each quarter
Hire the right people; train them in the standard; watch their work closely; punish the mistakes; reward the results at the end of the year
Plan the goals; organise the team; lead the people; control the results; repeat the cycle every month until the goal is reached
questions.why: This five-part plan is Exercise 2 and section 3 of the group project. See §7.8.

questions.stem: Analyse the restaurant owner who sees rising complaints, falling ratings and falling profits and says 'I think everything is fine'. Determine the problem.
options: The information was screaming; the manager was not looking — 'I think' instead of 'I know'
The restaurant had no data, so the owner had nothing to go on except his own impression
The customers were wrong, because ratings reflect mood more than the quality of the food
Profits are not a manager's concern; they belong to the accountant and the owner
questions.why: Customers vote with data and the manager answers with a feeling. See the answer to question 1 in §7.1.

questions.stem: Analyse the café whose satisfaction standard is 90% and this month's survey is 70%, with complaints clustering on weekday lunches about waiting. Determine the right corrective action.
options: Fix peak-hour staffing with a schedule — the cause — not a discount or a lecture
Offer a 20% discount to all customers so that the satisfaction score recovers quickly
Lecture the staff about being faster, since waiting is the complaint and speed is the answer
Lower the standard to 70%, since the café has clearly been unable to reach 90%
questions.why: Gap → cause → check → fix. The manager who skips 'cause' fixes the wrong thing with confidence. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Select the KPI that passes the KPI test for a gym.
options: Member retention ≥ 85% monthly, with visits per member per week ≥ 2.0 as the early warning
Number of likes on Instagram each week, which shows how many people are talking about the gym
The manager's number of meetings with staff each month, which shows how closely the gym is run
The number of new members signed up each month, which shows that the marketing is working
questions.why: Goal-connected, measurable from a real source, team-influenceable — and the visits KPI warns three months early. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Select the headline KPI for an airline.
options: Flight punctuality
Number of employees
Size of the head office
Head office size
questions.why: Punctuality is the visible heartbeat of a thousand coordinated operations; baggage accuracy and load factor support it. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a call centre that measures calls per hour and finds calls getting shorter and ruder. Determine the chapter's explanation.
options: People optimise the number, not the goal
The agents are lazy and use the target as an excuse to get rid of difficult customers
Customers now prefer short calls and reward the agents who end them quickly
The measurement system is broken and is recording the calls incorrectly
questions.why: The first of the three harms of too much measurement. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Analyse Nokia, which measured market share every quarter and never measured whether customers still wanted its phones. Determine the lesson.
options: Controlling only what is easy to count is the most comfortable way to fail
Market share is the wrong KPI for every company
Nokia should have measured market share more often, monthly rather than quarterly
Measurement caused the failure, so Nokia should have relied on managers' judgement instead
questions.why: The metric improved while the mission died. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Select the rewrite of 'your work is terrible' that is timely, constructive and specific.
options: 'Two of the five reports had calculation errors in the totals — let's review your checking step together before Thursday's report'
'You are not good at this job, and if the reports do not improve very soon we will have to talk about your future here'
'Try harder next time, check your work more carefully, and remember that the whole team depends on your numbers being right'
'Everyone makes mistakes, don't worry about it, the important thing is that you learn from this and keep going'
questions.why: Names the exact behaviour and the standard, aimed at the work and the future. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Analyse the feedback 'improve customer response time'. Determine what is missing.
options: Specificity — from what to what, by when
Timeliness — the feedback has come too late to change anything
Constructiveness — it attacks the person rather than the work
Nothing — it is good feedback that tells the team exactly what to do
questions.why: Half-good: constructive direction, but not specific. Rewrite: 'from 6 hours to 2 by month-end, start by acknowledging every ticket within 30 minutes.' See §7.5.

questions.stem: Classify a quality check before a product launch.
options: Feedforward control
Concurrent control
Feedback control
Not a form of control
questions.why: Stopping defects before customers exist is control before the work. See the table in §7.6.

questions.stem: Classify a barista trainer standing beside a new hire during the morning rush.
options: Concurrent control
Feedforward control
Feedback control
Over-control
questions.why: Correcting live, mid-work. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Classify reviewing last quarter's complaints to redesign the process.
options: Feedback control
Feedforward control
Concurrent control
Monitoring
questions.why: Learning from completed results — too late for this time, essential for the next. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Determine the defensible form of digital monitoring of employees.
options: Announced openly, work-related and proportionate — such as delivery locations during shifts
Secret tracking of personal devices, as long as the data is used only for work purposes
Keystroke counting of professionals, because it shows exactly how long they spend working
Any monitoring at all, as long as it improves the numbers the company reports
questions.why: Transparency decides; the test is the four questions and whether you would tell them. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who monitors a trained professional minute by minute. Determine the chapter's view.
options: It is not control — it is a Theory X announcement that kills initiative
It is good concurrent control, because problems are caught while the work is happening
It is feedforward control, because the monitoring prevents mistakes before they occur
It is required by law for professionals
questions.why: Over-control signals distrust and pushes the best people out. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Select the immediate fix and the system fix for the hotel with long check-in queues.
options: Immediate: a supervisor coaching the desk at peak hours (concurrent); system: online check-in and better rostering (feedforward)
Immediate: lower the room price for guests who waited; system: paint the lobby and add seating so the wait feels shorter
Immediate: replace the front desk staff who are too slow; system: hire new staff with hotel experience
Immediate: ignore it, because queues are normal at check-in; system: wait for the ratings to recover by themselves
questions.why: One immediate fix is usually concurrent control; one system fix is usually feedforward. See §7.8 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who, facing a 20-point satisfaction gap, immediately announces a discount without reading the survey details. Determine the step skipped.
options: Diagnosing the cause before acting
Setting the standard — the manager never defined what 'good' looked like
Measuring performance — the manager did not run the survey properly
Comparing results — the manager did not calculate the gap correctly
questions.why: Steps 1–3 were done; step 4's real question is what is CAUSING the gap. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Describe the link between planning and controlling.
options: Planning sets the goals; controlling checks the progress toward them
Planning and controlling are the same function seen at different times of the year
Controlling replaces planning once the organisation has been running for some time
Planning happens after controlling, because you need results before you can set goals
questions.why: Goals nobody checks are wishes. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Describe step 1 of the control process.
options: Set standards — define what 'good' looks like in numbers
Punish the slowest worker so that the rest of the team understands the standard
Write a report on the team's current performance
Hire an inspector who will check the work independently of the manager
questions.why: Standards are set during planning. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Explain why the control loop never ends.
options: Corrective action changes the standard or the work, which is then measured again
Managers like meetings and the control loop gives them a reason to hold one every month
Company rules require managers to report on the same KPIs every quarter
Customers demand it, because they want to see the company checking its own work
questions.why: Step 4 feeds back into step 1. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter says KPIs are 'the vital few'.
options: A few well-chosen measures tell the truth faster than many numbers
Companies cannot afford many measures, because every measure costs money to collect
Only top managers may see KPIs, so the list has to be short enough for a board meeting
KPIs are secret, so the fewer people who know them the better
questions.why: Measure the vital few. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Describe what happens to the unmeasured.
options: It quietly disappears because people focus on what is counted
It improves automatically because people are free to do it in their own way
It stays exactly the same, because measurement has no effect on behaviour
It becomes the most important work, because people prefer what is not checked
questions.why: The unmeasured disappears. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Explain the phrase 'measure the vital few — and go and look'.
options: Numbers say what happened; walking the floor shows why
Managers should count everything and then look at the numbers once a week
Looking replaces measuring, because an experienced manager can see the problems
Only data matters, and looking is for managers who do not trust the numbers
questions.why: Data says WHAT; it cannot say WHY. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Describe 'timely' feedback.
options: Feedback given close to the event, not months later
Feedback given once a year at the appraisal
Feedback given in public so that the whole team learns from it
Feedback given by email only, so that there is a written record
questions.why: Feedback about March delivered in December is archaeology. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Describe 'constructive' feedback.
options: Feedback aimed at the work and the future, not at the person
Feedback that is always positive so that the employee stays motivated
Feedback that lists every fault so that nothing is missed
Feedback given loudly so that the employee understands it is serious
questions.why: Constructive = aimed at the work, not the person. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Describe 'specific' feedback.
options: Feedback that names the exact behaviour and the standard expected
Feedback that says 'try harder' so that the employee knows more effort is needed
Feedback that covers everything at once so that the employee has the full picture
Feedback with no examples, so that the employee is not embarrassed by details
questions.why: Specific names the behaviour and the standard. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Describe concurrent control.
options: Correcting work while it happens
Preventing problems before work starts
Learning from completed results
Checking the yearly budget
questions.why: Concurrent = during. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Describe feedback control.
options: Learning from completed results to improve the next time
Stopping defects before customers exist by checking the inputs
Coaching live during the rush while the work is being done
Setting standards during planning
questions.why: Feedback control is after the work. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Explain what 'tight on outcomes, loose on method' means.
options: Measure the result the customer feels; let the trained person choose how
Control every step of every task so that the result is guaranteed
Control nothing and trust the team to deliver whatever it can
Measure only the method, because a good method always produces a good result
questions.why: Better-placed control, not less control. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Describe the Nokia lesson.
options: Measuring only the easy number (market share) hid that customers no longer wanted the phones
Nokia measured too little and should have added more KPIs to its dashboard
Nokia had no managers who understood control, so nobody checked the numbers
Nokia's KPIs were perfect, but the market changed too fast for any control system
questions.why: Controlling only what is easy to count is the most comfortable way to fail. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Explain why over-control pushes the best people out.
options: Minute-by-minute monitoring signals distrust and kills initiative
The best people hate all rules
Over-control costs too much money, so the company cannot afford to pay the best people
It makes work too easy, so the best people become bored and look for a challenge
questions.why: Over-control is a Theory X announcement. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Describe the 'monitoring line you will not cross' in a control plan.
options: A written limit on how closely people are watched, to protect trust
A line on the factory floor that visitors and inspectors may not cross
The maximum budget the manager may spend on monitoring software
The deadline by which the control plan must be completed and approved
questions.why: The control plan names a monitoring line. See §7.8.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between an immediate fix and a system fix.
options: An immediate fix corrects today's gap; a system fix stops it returning
They are the same, and the chapter uses both names for the same corrective action
A system fix is cheaper and faster, so it should always be tried first
An immediate fix is permanent, while a system fix lasts only until the next review
questions.why: Immediate (usually concurrent) and system (usually feedforward). See §7.8.

questions.stem: Identify what each KPI in a control plan must have.
options: A standard, a source and a frequency
A manager's signature and a date
A colour on the dashboard and a trend arrow
A bonus attached to it for the team that hits it
questions.why: Each KPI needs a standard, source and frequency. See §7.8.

questions.stem: Determine the right first question when a café's rating drops from 4.6 to 3.9.
options: Why did it drop?
Who should we fire?
Can we hide the rating?
Should we close?
questions.why: Ask why, not who. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a team that hides bad numbers from the manager. Determine the likely cause.
options: Measurement there means punishment, so people hide numbers instead of improving them
The team is dishonest by nature and would hide the numbers whatever the manager did
The numbers are not important, so the team does not bother to report them accurately
The manager asked too often, so the team stopped taking the requests seriously
questions.why: A punishment culture produces hidden numbers. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Classify a small leak found and fixed on day one.
options: Cheap — a problem found early
Catastrophic — a problem found late
Not a control issue
A planning failure
questions.why: Leaks are cheap early, catastrophic late. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Determine the step when a manager compares this month's 70% satisfaction with the 90% standard.
options: Step 3 — compare results
Step 1 — set standards
Step 2 — measure performance
Step 4 — take corrective action
questions.why: Comparing results to the standard is step 3. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Select the corrective action for a gap caused by peak-hour understaffing.
options: Change the staffing schedule for peak hours
Give every customer a discount until the satisfaction score recovers
Lower the standard so that the current performance is within target
Lecture the staff about working faster during the lunch rush
questions.why: Fix the cause. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Select the leading indicator for a university worried about dropouts.
options: Class attendance in the first weeks
The number of students who graduated last year
The size of the campus and the number of lecture halls
The number of applications received for next year
questions.why: Attendance warns before the dropout happens. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Classify 'number of Instagram likes' as a KPI for a bakery's profit goal.
options: Fails the test — not clearly connected to the goal
Passes — it is measurable
Passes — it is something the bakery's team can influence
Passes all three tests and should be on the dashboard
questions.why: Connected to the goal is the first test. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a school that rewards teachers only on exam pass rates and finds they teach only exam tricks. Determine the explanation.
options: People optimise the number, not the goal
Teachers are lazy and take the shortest route to the reward
Exams are too easy, so tricks are enough to pass them
Rewards never work in education, because teachers are not motivated by money
questions.why: The metric improved while the mission died. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Select the manager's move after the dashboard shows a problem.
options: Go and look at the work to understand why
Add three more KPIs so that the dashboard shows the problem in more detail
Punish the department responsible so that the numbers improve next month
Wait for next month's numbers to see whether the problem corrects itself
questions.why: Data says what; go and look for why. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Determine the harm when a manager checks every employee's screen every hour.
options: Constant monitoring signals distrust
It improves creativity, because employees know their work is being seen
It is good feedforward control, because mistakes are caught before they happen
It is harmless, because employees who are working have nothing to hide
questions.why: Signals distrust — the third harm. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Classify 'your work is terrible' as feedback.
options: Not constructive, not specific
Timely and specific, because it is given straight after the work
Constructive but late, because it should have been given earlier
Perfect feedback, because it tells the employee exactly how the manager feels
questions.why: It attacks the person and names nothing. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Select the timely moment for feedback on a presentation.
options: The same day, in private
At the annual review, where all feedback is collected together
Six months later, when the manager has seen several more presentations
Never — presentations are personal and feedback would be discouraging
questions.why: Feedback close to the event. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Classify checking the ingredients before cooking starts.
options: Feedforward control
Concurrent control
Feedback control
No form of control
questions.why: Prevention before the work. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Select the control that is 'better placed' for a trained delivery rider.
options: Measure on-time delivery and customer rating; let the rider choose the route
Track every turn and call the rider every ten minutes to check progress
No measurement at all, because a trained rider knows the job better than the manager
Measure only the route taken, because the right route guarantees the right result
questions.why: Tight on outcomes, loose on method. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Select the three vital-few KPIs for a café aiming at happy customers.
options: Satisfaction score, average wait time, repeat visits
Number of chairs, wall colour and staff birthdays
Instagram likes, logo size and menu length
Rent, tax and insurance paid each month
questions.why: KPIs connected to the goal, measurable and influenceable. See §7.8.

questions.stem: Determine the feedback rule in a control plan for a hotel front desk.
options: Weekly, private, specific feedback to each receptionist
A public ranking of receptionists updated every hour on the staff noticeboard
Feedback once a year at the formal appraisal meeting
No feedback, so that receptionists feel trusted to do the job
questions.why: A feedback rule is part of the plan. See §7.8.

questions.stem: Classify a system fix that adds online check-in to stop queues.
options: Feedforward control
Concurrent control
Feedback control
Over-control that signals distrust
questions.why: System fixes are usually feedforward. See §7.8.
